chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadala ibn Ayyub from Isma'il ibn Abi Ziyad from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from his father (peace be upon him) from Ali (peace be upon him) who said:

When the child is capable of fasting for three consecutive days, then fasting the month of Ramadan becomes obligatory upon him. The approach in this narration is to understand that it is obligatory upon him for the sake of discipline (ta'dib), and although it is expressed with the wording of obligation (wujub), it is according to a type of concession, because it is appropriate that the child be made to fast when he is capable, to the extent of his capacity, so that he may become accustomed.
ai.seo_question: At what age or stage of capability does fasting become obligatory for a child in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In al-istibsar, Shaykh al-Tusi presents this narration to clarify the transition from voluntary practice to legal obligation for children (sibyan). The scholars interpret the 'obligation' (wujub) here as a preparatory discipline (tadib) to accustom the child to the fast, rather than the strict binding obligation (wujhab) applicable to adults, ensuring the child builds stamina gradually.
